title: Building Fractions from Unit Fractions
trouble: Students read the numerator and denominator as two separate whole numbers instead of one amount.

blocks.html: A unit fraction is one piece. Now we put pieces together. $\frac{3}{4}$ means 3 pieces, each of size $\frac{1}{4}$.

blocks.name: fractionbar
blocks.cap: Tap parts to shade them. Shade 3 of the 4 equal parts to show three fourths.

blocks.html: The bottom number (the denominator) tells the size of each piece: fourths. The top number (the numerator) counts how many of those pieces you have. So $\frac{3}{4}$ is one amount, "three fourths," just as "3 apples" is one amount: the 3 counts and the fourths say what is being counted.

head: Fraction

blocks.cap: The numerator counts; the denominator names the piece.

blocks.title: Shaded parts
blocks.q: A circle is cut into 8 equal parts and 5 are shaded. What fraction is shaded?

blocks.title: Count the pieces
blocks.q: How many pieces of size $\frac{1}{6}$ make $\frac{4}{6}$?

blocks.title: What is left?
blocks.q: 3 of 5 equal parts are shaded. What fraction is not shaded?
steps: Each part is $\frac{1}{5}$, so 2 parts make $\frac{2}{5}$.

blocks.html: Reading the two numbers separately. $\frac{3}{4}$ is not "3 and 4" and it is not bigger than 3. It is one number, less than 1: three of the four equal parts. Say it aloud as "three fourths" to keep it together.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 3, 3.NF.A.1 (understand a/b as the quantity formed by a parts of size 1/b)
